clue.text: Bonhomie of the Beak

parts.note: the good cheer is that of a bird's bill, which chirps merrily, not the geniality of a magistrate on the bench

explanation.surface: A stern magistrate shows unexpected good humour from the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beak' is British slang for a magistrate, which is the picture the surface paints; here it is a bird's bill, and cheerfulness in a bird is chirping.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerful liveliness is a form of good fellowship, and the word comes from the cheery cheep of a small bird.

clue.text: Takes a century to irrigate without a sluice says Curlylocks

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the word for a sluice is taken out of irrigate

parts.note: a sluice gate holds back water, so a sluice is a gate

explanation.surface: A curly-haired child grumbles that watering without a sluice will take a hundred years.
explanation.walkthrough: Curlylocks is the curly-haired figure of a nursery rhyme; her curls stand for the answer, the plural of cirrus, a curl or tendril.
explanation.definitionFit: Cirrus means a curl or tendril, so the plural describes curly locks of hair.

clue.text: In effect, one pie in a hundred ain't half started

parts.note: a law that is in effect is in, in force
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: half here takes the last two of the four letters of ain't

explanation.surface: A cockney complains that barely one pie in a hundred has even been begun.
explanation.definitionFit: Something incipient is only beginning, just started and not yet developed.

clue.text: Minced fruit with a glass of light

definitions.note: an adjective here for mincing, prim speech, where the answer is a phrase that names such speech

parts.note: prunes are dried plums, a fruit
with means together with, and
a prism is a glass block that splits light into colours

explanation.surface: Chopped fruit served alongside a glass of something light.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Little Dorrit, Mrs General says repeating 'papa, potatoes, poultry, prunes and prism' gives a pretty, prim form to the lips; 'minced' means spoken in that affected way.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase stands for affected, prissy speech, and mincing speech is exactly that prim affectation.

clue.text: To a Scot odourlessly 2

definitions.note: 2 stands for the answer to 2 Down, meaning just beginning

indicators.note: in Scots speech the word no becomes na, so this vowel changes as a Scot would say it

parts.note: odourlessly means with no smell at all, no scent

explanation.surface: Something smells of nothing to a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' points to 2 Down, whose meaning, just started, defines this answer too.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something at its very beginning, newly coming into existence.

clue.text: Hold it to hold sway

parts.note: a monarch carries this ornamental staff as the sign of sovereign power, so holding it means ruling

explanation.surface: Advice on keeping control: grip something and you will be in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: This ornamented rod is carried by a king or queen as the emblem of royal authority.

clue.text: The fashion as 27 knows of featherheaded youth

annotationWithheld.clue: The fashion as 27 knows of featherheaded youth

clue.text: Well locked ?

parts.note: well supplied with locks of hair, not securely fastened with a key

explanation.surface: Something is securely bolted shut.
explanation.definitionFit: Hirsute means having plenty of hair, and locks are tresses of hair.

clue.text: Talked of abridging the Lady of the Lake in poetry

indicators.note: abridging shortens the name, cutting it down to its first syllable

parts.note: Lake Constance shares its name with the woman's name Constance, so she is the lake's lady
versed can mean put into verse, so rendered in poetry

explanation.surface: Someone discussed cutting down Scott's long poem The Lady of the Lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Scott's poem; instead the lady is Constance, as in Lake Constance, cut to CON by 'abridging'.
explanation.definitionFit: To converse is to talk together, so conversed is a past tense meaning talked.

clue.text: Johnson's infernal flags

parts.note: Dr Johnson said hell is paved with these, and flags are paving stones, so they pave the infernal regions

explanation.surface: Banners connected with someone named Johnson and the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flags' suggests banners but means flagstones; Samuel Johnson is credited with 'Hell is paved with good intentions'.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-meant aims that come to nothing are proverbially the paving of hell, in Johnson's saying.

clue.text: Wins back the battered rose cup

indicators.note: something battered is knocked out of shape, so the letters of rose and cup are beaten into a new order

explanation.surface: A trophy in the shape of a rose gets dented while being reclaimed.
explanation.definitionFit: To recoup is to regain or recover what was lost, as a gambler does with lost stakes.

clue.text: College boy collared

parts.note: a pupil of the Berkshire college whose boys once wore the broad stiff white collar named after it, not a boy arrested by police

explanation.surface: A schoolboy is caught and nabbed by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collared' suggests an arrest; it means wearing the famous collar of a particular school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil of the famous school by Windsor is so called, and its broad starched collar was a mark of its boys.

clue.text: There's a tool to perform this

definitions.meaning: an instrument or utensil used for doing a job
to carry out or put into effect, as with a plan or policy

explanation.surface: Someone points out the instrument needed for a task.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the word is an instrument for work; as a verb it means to put a decision into practice.

clue.text: He did not illustrate his namesake's stories

definitions.text: He did not illustrate his namesake's stories

parts.words: He did not illustrate his namesake's stories
parts.note: Richard ..., the Victorian Punch artist, shared a surname with his nephew, creator of Sherlock Holmes, yet never drew pictures for those tales

explanation.surface: An artist declined to draw pictures for a writer sharing his name.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard 'Dicky' Doyle drew the famous Punch cover; his nephew Arthur Conan Doyle wrote the Sherlock Holmes stories, which other artists illustrated.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to the Punch illustrator Richard and to his nephew Arthur Conan, author of the Holmes stories.

clue.text: Knead bread for a city

indicators.note: kneading works dough over and over, so the letters of bread are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A baker's instruction to work the dough, oddly attached to a town.
explanation.definitionFit: Breda is a fortified city in the southern Netherlands, famous for its siege.

clue.text: Bottle for a sailor after coaling?

parts.note: anyone who has just loaded coal is covered in soot, black
Jack, as in Jack tar, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A drink for a seaman who has just finished loading coal.
explanation.definitionFit: A blackjack was an old leather drinking vessel coated with tar, a kind of jug or bottle.

clue.text: A lot stouter than pine-needles

parts.note: pine-needles might be called a tree's nails; the real wooden pins that fasten ships' timbers are much thicker

explanation.surface: Something is compared for thickness with the needles of a pine.
explanation.walkthrough: Shipwrights fastened planks with long hardwood pegs; the clue treats pine-needles as a tree's slender nails to set up the comparison.
explanation.definitionFit: These are wooden pegs used to fasten planks in shipbuilding, far thicker than any needle.

clue.text: I camber it so as to overlap

indicators.note: so as means arranged in such a way, so the letters of I camber it are set out differently

explanation.surface: A builder curves a surface so that its parts lie over one another.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiles or scales that imbricate lie in overlapping rows, like roof tiles.

clue.text: Anticipates earlier fruits?

parts.note: ante is Latin for before, so it means earlier, as in ante-room
dates are the fruits of the date palm

explanation.surface: Someone looks forward to the first fruits of the season.
explanation.definitionFit: To antedate something is to come before it or forestall it, which is to anticipate it.

clue.text: Trout fisher ?

parts.note: one who catches trout by stroking their bellies by hand until they can be flipped out of the water

explanation.surface: Someone who angles for trout.
explanation.walkthrough: Poachers catch trout by hand, stroking under the fish until it relaxes; the practice is called tickling.
explanation.definitionFit: A poacher who catches fish by hand, gently stroking them, is one who tickles them.

clue.text: Old brass which Falstaff would have taken without objection

parts.note: sack, a dry white wine, is the drink Shakespeare's Falstaff swills
a but is an objection, as in no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: An antique trumpet that Falstaff would have accepted without demur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' suggests money or metal but means a brass instrument; Falstaff drinks sack, a Spanish white wine, and would take it with no 'but' at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The sackbut is the early trombone, an old instrument of the brass family.

clue.text: Take me back and tuck me in

definitions.text: Take me back and tuck me in

indicators.note: back says the little word me is turned to read the other way

parts.note: to bed someone is to tuck them in for the night

explanation.surface: A tired child asks to be carried home and put to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To embed something is to fix it firmly in a surrounding mass, much as tucking in sets a sleeper snugly in the sheets.

clue.text: Biblical tent-dweller

parts.note: the Bible speaks of the black tents of this son of Ishmael and his nomad people, as in the Song of Songs

explanation.surface: A nomad of scripture living under canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: Kedar was a son of Ishmael whose desert tribe lived in tents, mentioned in Psalm 120 and the Song of Songs.

clue.text: Senior ditto essential to trade in Tokyo

parts.note: do is the abbreviation for ditto
the yen is the currency of Japan, needed for any trade in its capital

explanation.surface: An elder repeats that business in Japan depends on him.
explanation.definitionFit: A doyen is the most senior or respected member of a group.

clue.text: Drinks at "The Feathers"

parts.note: a pub name in the surface, but the plumes on a rooster's rear are feathers too, so mixed drinks are named after them

explanation.surface: A round is ordered at a pub called The Feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Feathers' is a common British pub name; read as plain feathers it describes a rooster's tail plumes.
explanation.definitionFit: Mixed spirits drinks take the name, and a rooster's tail plumes are literally feathers.

clue.text: Players to be drilled ?

definitions.meaning: tennis players ranked in advance so the best do not meet early in a tournament
a farmer sows grain in drills, so what is drilled is planted grain

explanation.surface: Sportsmen about to be put through their training.
explanation.definitionFit: Top-ranked competitors in a draw share the name with kernels that a farmer plants in furrows.

clue.text: Sailor gets his girly back, being very deep

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor

indicators.note: back says the word for the girl is turned to read the other way

parts.note: a lassy, another spelling of lassie, is a girl, a girly

explanation.surface: A sailor wins back his sweetheart, his feelings running very deep.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes the ocean's deepest zones, so it means extremely deep; 'being' makes the definition read as a description.

clue.text: Fine stuff from a rebel's brother.

parts.note: Jack Cade led a popular revolt in Kent in 1450, so he is the rebel

explanation.surface: Some fine possession comes from the brother of an insurgent.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the rebel first but the brother comes first in the answer; Jack Cade is the English rebel of Shakespeare's Henry VI Part 2.
explanation.definitionFit: Brocade is a rich woven fabric with raised patterns, so fine cloth or stuff.

clue.text: They are against everything but old coins

definitions.text: They are against everything but old coins

parts.words: They are against everything but old coins
parts.note: people who object to all things, except that split after three letters they are in favour of testers, the old English sixpences

explanation.surface: Grumblers who oppose everything except old money.
explanation.walkthrough: A tester (teston) was an old English silver coin, later a sixpence; PRO means in favour of, so the answer split after its third letter favours those coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Objectors who demonstrate are, by definition, people who oppose something.
